extracted.intended_audience: academics, administrative-law scholars, policymakers, and financial regulators (SEC, CFTC, FSOC, OIRA)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative/analytic criteria for performing, reviewing, and institutionally organizing cost-benefit analysis (CBA) of financial regulation, with emphasis on institutional capacity, macroeconomic modeling, interagency review, and judicial implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility of quantified CBA in finance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether ‘precise, reliable quantifiable’ cost-benefit analysis of financial regulation is feasible (debated between critics like Coates who find it currently unfeasible and defenders like Sunstein, Posner & Weyl who argue it is feasible or can be made so).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the debate; do not assume impossibility—consider investing in methods and institutional arrangements to improve feasibility rather than abandoning quantification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional capacity to perform high-quality CBA
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent financial regulatory agencies currently ‘lack the capacity to do cost-benefit analyses of acceptable quality’ compared to Executive Branch agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improve internal capacity through hiring economists, creating dedicated analytic units, and learning from Executive Branch models (e.g., EPA, OIRA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of macroeconomic (general-equilibrium) models
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial regulation often requires macroeconomic assessments (how banking restrictions affect economy-wide crisis probability) rather than microeconomic analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When regulation may produce meaningful indirect or economy-wide consequences, use a general equilibrium framework (e.g., CGE) rather than partial-equilibrium techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice between partial-equilibrium and economy-wide modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Select modeling approach based on expected scope: partial-equilibrium OK for narrow, sector-specific impacts; CGE or other economy-wide models needed for large, economy-wide effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh costs and benefits of big-modeling (data, peer review, expertise) against the risk of missing indirect effects; follow EPA Guidelines on when to apply whole-economy models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of computable general equilibrium (CGE) modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: CGE modeling can estimate impacts of policies expected to have large, economy-wide effects by 'shocking' the model and comparing equilibria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ CGE to forecast long-run, economy-wide impacts and distributional effects, but account for limitations (poor fit for short-run transitional costs or narrow geographic/sectoral policies) and ensure appropriate specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review and transparency of modeling methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Models and macroeconomic analyses should be subject to peer review (as EPA has done) and transparency demands (e.g., Senate pressures for disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish expert panels, release white papers, and subject models to external peer review to increase credibility and usability in rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in research and federal funding for methodological development
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic techniques for valuing regulatory benefits in finance are underdeveloped and require research investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support academic research and federal funding to develop macro-financial valuation techniques analogous to those developed for environmental regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breakeven and sensitivity analysis when full quantification is infeasible
rubrics_metrics.description: When certain valuations are highly uncertain, agencies should perform breakeven analysis (e.g., 'how high the benefits would have to be to justify the costs') and sensitivity analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use breakeven/sensitivity to discipline judgment under uncertainty and to show thresholds required for regulatory justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating distributional impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: CGE and other economy-wide models can estimate distributional impacts of policy shocks on household groups or industrial sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include distributional analysis where relevant to inform equity implications and political economy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of macroeconomic models for short-run transitional costs
rubrics_metrics.description: CGE and similar models are ill-suited to analyzing short-run transitional costs without proper specification and are costly for narrow-impact analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplement CGE with short-run or sector-specific methods when transitional or localized impacts matter; document limitations explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of a Statistical Life (VSL) and valuation best-practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory valuation exercises (e.g., NRC’s VSL update) must follow sound empirical methods for benefit valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly update valuation metrics (like VSL) using best available evidence and transparent methodologies; subject updates to peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of economists into policymaking processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding economists into rulemaking (e.g., SEC’s Division of Economic and Risk Analysis) improves quantification and rule quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create and empower economic-analysis units within agencies and integrate them into decision-making to produce more defensible CBAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interagency coordination and centralized expertise (FSOC/OIRA models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralized coordinating bodies (e.g., FSOC, OIRA, Interagency Working Group for social cost of carbon) can diffuse macroeconomic expertise and harmonize analytic standards across agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empower FSOC or a similar body to coordinate macroeconomic modeling for financial regulators and to replicate successful interagency practices (e.g., social cost of carbon approach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of OIRA in reviewing significant rules
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA’s review of significant federal regulations provides oversight, standardization, and incentives for better analysis; extending an OIRA-like role to independent agencies could improve CBA quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider formal mechanisms (Executive Order or statutory change) to allow OIRA review or OIRA-like interagency review of independent financial regulators' CBAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review does not displace judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: An Executive Order cannot eliminate otherwise-available judicial review; agencies preparing CBAs for OIRA review remain subject to judicial challenge of their analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not design institutional reforms assuming OIRA review will substitute for courts; ensure CBAs are legally defensible under APA review standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review as an information-forcing mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review compels agencies to produce reasoned explanations and sufficient scientific references, improving regulatory records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare thorough administrative records anticipating judicial scrutiny; rigorous executive oversight can make courts more deferential, but agencies should not forgo quality expecting shelter from courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference tied to executive oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are more likely to be deferential to agency CBAs if there is evidence of rigorous Executive Branch (OIRA) vetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use robust executive vetting to signal quality and obtain more deferential judicial review; document OIRA engagement in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective review and peer review processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls to institutionalize retrospective analysis of rules and to use peer review to improve future rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement procedures for post-implementation review and corrective analysis to learn from outcomes and refine models and assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory triggers for conducting CBA
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory language (e.g., requirement to ‘consider or determine whether an action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest’ or repeated 'necessary or appropriate' language in Dodd-Frank) increases the need for CBA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where statutes use open-ended standards, agencies should prepare thorough CBAs to demonstrate consideration of costs and benefits and to withstand judicial scrutiny (post-Michigan v. EPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid insulating CBAs from judicial challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to have Executive Branch review replace judicial review (or to make CBAs non-reviewable) are legally and practically infeasible under APA and separation-of-powers principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions recognizing courts will remain able to review CBAs; focus on improving analytic quality rather than exempting analyses from review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical assistance from centralized review offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent agencies (e.g., CFTC) requesting technical help from OIRA demonstrates a need for centralized technical assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide avenues for technical assistance (methodological support, data, model implementation) from OIRA or other central bodies to agencies lacking capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit statement of model limitations and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must disclose model specifications, assumptions, and limitations (e.g., CGE suitability, nonstationarity of finance) in their analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make assumptions explicit, run sensitivity checks, and explain how model choices affect conclusions to make analyses transparent and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing nonstationarity and innovation in finance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because finance is 'non-stationary' and subject to rapid innovation and shocks, CBAs must grapple with changing relationships over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate scenario analysis, robustness checks, and forward-looking modeling to account for innovation and regime shifts in financial markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on normative/opaque inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics warn that financial-system CBAs can be driven by normatively controversial or opaque inputs that entrench status quo preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure normative choices are transparent, justify value weightings, and where possible ground inputs in empirical evidence rather than unexamined assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of regulatory management procedures (e.g., retrospective analysis, peer and congressional review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional frameworks for CBA should include judicial, congressional, and peer review and retrospective analysis as part of future regulatory processes (as AEI suggested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt multi-layered review (executive, peer, retrospective) to improve CBA quality and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional limits on agency independence vis-à-vis CBA processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of for-cause removal protections should not be invoked to expand independence beyond what Congress provided in order to avoid executive vetting of CBAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate functional arguments that allow executive oversight of analytic quality without undermining statutory independence beyond Congress's intent.
